Threat follows Estonia’s decision to close border with Russia for six months from 1 December

Russia has threatened Estonia with “open war”, accusing the Nato and EU member state of a series of hostile actions, including allowing Ukrainian drones to use its airspace to attack Russian targets.

The threat follows Estonia’s announcement that it will close its border crossings with Russia for at least six months from 1 December, after accusing Russian security services of attempting to set fire to an Estonian defence company.

Moscow summoned an Estonian envoy on Monday and told him that “such provocative and extremely dangerous actions are on the verge of triggering open war with Russia”.

Separately, Russia threatened “painful consequences” after Ukraine confirmed it carried out devastating strikes on two Russian ships at a port in Libya.

Ukraine sank a Russian naval corvette using naval drones in Benghazi and also hit the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which president Volodymyr Zelensky claimed had been used to transport weapons.

A Russian Ka-27 helicopter was also destroyed along with the corvette, Zelensky said.

The attack came only a day after a drone strike on a Russian-military linked cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland.

Disruptions to major shipping routes linked to wars in the Middle East and Ukraine could increase the World Food Programme’s operating costs by $727m by mid-2027, potentially putting food assistance for an additional 7.3 million people at risk.

WFP executive director Luke Lindberg warned that maritime chokepoints and restrictions on food exports were increasing pressure on global food supply chains. Climate-related disruptions, including those associated with El Nino, could further compound the problem.

“It’s an unthinkable scenario, and it could not come at a worse time,” Lindberg said.

He urged diplomats to work towards rapid solutions to ensure that 10 million tonnes of Ukrainian and Russian grain already held in silos could reach people in need.

A Russian drone briefly entered Polish airspace during an attack on Ukraine, Poland’s military warned on Tuesday.

The alleged incursion comes after officials said that three Russian Kh-101 missiles landed in Poland on Friday, deepening concerns that the war could spill over into Nato territory.

A Russian unmanned aerial vehicle briefly entered Polish airspace during a nighttime attack on western Ukraine, Poland’s armed forces have said, marking another aerial incursion into the Nato territory.

Polish authorities said permission had been granted to shoot down the object. However, the military decided against using weapons after the drone changed course and began moving eastwards.

The armed forces said the decision was made “taking into account the potential threat to civilians and the possible consequences of shooting down the object”.

The incident comes after three Russian Kh-101 missiles landed in Poland on Friday, raising concerns about the potential spillover of Russia’s war against Ukraine into neighbouring Nato countries.

US ​defence secretary Pete Hegseth has yet to approve the transfer of about 60 Patriot air defence interceptors that Washington had already agreed to supply to Ukraine, the Financial ⁠Times reported today.

Ukraine has repeatedly said it urgently needs more missile interceptors to counter growing Russian missile and drone attacks. The interceptors include US-made PAC-3 and PAC-2 missiles, some ⁠of which are held in ​European ⁠arsenals and are being financed by Kyiv's Western allies, the newspaper said.

The outstanding allocation includes PAC-3 ‌interceptors scheduled for delivery between September and December, the FT said, adding that none of those shipments has yet been ‌approved for transfer.

A further 20 or so PAC-2 interceptors, an older variant, have reportedly also been allocated to Ukraine but are awaiting approval for delivery. The FT also reported that ⁠a separate effort to secure US approval for Ukraine to produce its own Patriot interceptors has been delayed at the Pentagon.

Last month, the US approved a sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Ukraine valued at about $2.1 billion, although deliveries are not expected until the early 2030s

A Pentagon spokesperson told the FT there had been no change in US policy regarding support for Ukraine, while declining to comment further on the weapons. "The Department of War has pursued ‌multiple parallel lines of effort to accelerate transatlantic industrial ​co-operation on the Patriot air and missile defence system ‌with European partners and Ukraine, ⁠and continues that work to this day," the ⁠official was quoted as saying.

Germany has said it is taking seriously reports that Russia may launch a nuclear-armed satellite, identified as Sputnik-S, into orbit later this year.

Germany’s foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), and its armed forces have shared intelligence indicating that a Russian satellite named Sputnik-S was assembled several years ago and is based in the Moscow region, broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung reported.

If confirmed, the deployment would violate international treaties prohibiting nuclear weapons in orbit.

Moscow has dismissed the reports as “unfounded allegations” and denied having plans to deploy nuclear weapons in space.

Volodymyr Zelensky urged Nato to admit Ukraine as a member, arguing that full alliance membership would provide more reliable security guarantees after the war with Russia.

Addressing the Nato Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin yesterday, he said Ukraine could also contribute its battlefield experience and military technology to the alliance.

"Wouldn't it be more effective to simply admit Ukraine into Nato? Wouldn't that be better for all of us, for everyone? Wouldn't it be more feasible? And wouldn't it be more reliable when it comes to actually guaranteeing security?" he said.

Nato secretary general Mark Rutte said membership remained a decision for the alliance, but acknowledged that not all member states currently supported Ukraine’s accession.

German chancellor Friedrich Merz said it had been a mistake not to admit Ukraine at the 2008 Bucharest summit.

"Today, looking back, we can all see what a mistake it was not to support the American proposal at the 2008 Nato summit in Bucharest to admit Ukraine to Nato.

"If it had become a member of Nato, this war could probably have been prevented."

An investigation reportedly based on more than 11 million leaked Russian death certificates has identified 1,087 Russian military personnel who died by suicide since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Guardian – which analysed confidential data from Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat – has revealed that a further 885 military deaths in or near Ukraine were classified as firearm-related injuries of “undetermined intent”, a category experts say may conceal additional suicides.

The figures, which analysts believe underestimate the true toll, show recorded military suicides rising from more than 50 in 2022 to 365 in 2025. The data also records nearly 300 suicides in 2026, although the year’s figures remain incomplete.

“There’s clearly a lot of coercion used by the Russian military to force people to go forward. In some cases, they will abuse them, torture them, use different types of physical abuse,” Rob Lee, a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute told the outlet.

“So it’s not surprising that some guys commit suicide,” he added.

Russia has warned Estonia that its actions risk triggering an “open war”, accusing the Baltic country of pursuing an increasingly hostile policy towards Moscow.
